analysis.one_liner: Makes wartime contractor fraud and profiteering a federal crime carrying up to 20 years in prison and forfeiture of illegal profits.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared the Senate Judiciary Committee and was placed on the Senate calendar in May 2007, but it never received a Senate vote before the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill made it a federal crime to defraud the United States or overcharge it in connection with a war, military action, or relief and reconstruction work. Convictions could bring up to 20 years in prison and a fine equal to twice the illegal profits, and the government could seize property tied to the fraud. It was written in response to fraud by contractors on Iraq and Afghanistan-related work, passed the Senate Judiciary Committee with amendments, and was placed on the Senate calendar — but the full Senate never voted on it before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers who fund war and reconstruction contracts, since fraud and overbilling would carry prison terms of up to 20 years, fines of up to twice the illegal profits, and seizure of the proceeds — money that could be recovered for the public. Honest contractors also benefit from a market where competitors cannot win by overbilling the government.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers funding war and reconstruction contracts

how_it_helps.text: It made it a federal crime to run a scheme to defraud the United States, or to overvalue goods or services with intent to defraud, in connection with a war, military action, or relief and reconstruction activities — punishable by up to 20 years in prison [S2][S3].
It set the fine at the greater of $1 million or twice the gross profits from the offense, so a fraudulent contractor could not simply keep the gains [S2][S3].

It allowed the government to seize property traceable to the offense through civil and criminal forfeiture, and made the offense a predicate crime for racketeering (RICO) and money laundering prosecutions [S3].
It gave federal prosecutors extraterritorial jurisdiction and broader venue options, so fraud committed overseas in a war zone could be prosecuted in U.S. courts [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Contractors and their executives who defraud the government in connection with military action or reconstruction, who would face criminal prosecution, fines of twice their gross profits, and forfeiture of proceeds. Enforcement costs fall on the Justice Department and the court system.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fraudulent war contractors and their executives

drawbacks.text: The original bill criminalized overvaluing goods or services "with the specific intent to defraud and excessively profit," and critics could argue that "excessive profit" is a vague standard that could chill legitimate contractors from aggressive but legal pricing; the committee amendment struck that phrase, narrowing the crime to fraud with intent to defraud [S3][S4].
Additional views were filed with the committee report, signaling that not all members agreed with the bill as reported [S6].

The bill added new tools — extraterritorial jurisdiction, broader venue, and forfeiture — that expand federal prosecutorial power generally, which carries a cost whenever prosecutorial discretion is widened beyond war contracting to any fraud connected to relief or reconstruction activities [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real: wartime contracting involves enormous public spending with weak oversight, and the bill would have given prosecutors a purpose-built fraud charge, profit-based fines, and forfeiture tools aimed at a documented problem. The main drawback — that "profiteering" could be defined too vaguely and chill legitimate contracting — was serious enough that the committee itself softened the bill, striking the "excessive profit" intent language before reporting it [S3][S4]. Even so, the amended bill never got a floor vote, so whatever deterrence value it offered was never tested.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Judiciary Committee approved it and put it on the Senate's waiting list for floor action, but the Senate never voted on it before the two-year Congress ran out.

narrative.text: Senator Leahy introduced the bill on January 4, 2007, and it was referred to the Judiciary Committee [S1][S6].
Twenty-one Democratic senators signed on as cosponsors; no Republican cosponsor appears on the bill's cosponsor page [S5].
The Judiciary Committee held hearings on January 31 and March 20, 2007, then ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment on April 25, 2007 [S6].

On May 15, 2007, the committee reported the bill with amendments and a written report, and it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders — the Senate's waiting list for floor consideration [S6].
No further action was ever taken: the bill sat on the calendar without a Senate vote, and all action ceased when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: War contractors who might have faced prosecution, twice-profit fines, and forfeiture under the new law were spared it, because the bill never reached a vote. Taxpayers funding wartime contracts gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Contractors who escaped new fraud liability

for.name: Sen. Patrick Leahy
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, chaired committee hearings on it in January and March 2007, and reported it to the Senate with amendments in May 2007 [S1][S6].

for.name: Senate Committee on the Judiciary
for.what_they_did: Held two hearings, ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment on April 25, 2007, and filed written report No. 110-66 [S6].

for.name: 21 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Sens. Clinton, Kerry, Feingold, Boxer, Durbin, and Byrd [S5].

against.name: Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: As leader of the Democratic majority that controlled the Senate floor, never brought the bill up for a vote; it sat on the legislative calendar until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 22 Senate supporters — the sponsor and 21 cosponsors — were Democrats, and no Republican signed on; the bill cleared the Democratic-run Judiciary Committee but never reached the floor for a vote [S5][S6].

industries.note: The bill exposed contractors working on wars and reconstruction to up to 20 years in prison, fines of twice their gross profits, forfeiture of proceeds, and RICO and money-laundering liability for fraud. Firms whose business model involved overbilling the government on war contracts stood to lose the most.

Legitimate contractors would have faced a new criminal statute and expanded prosecutorial tools aimed at their industry, but also a more level playing field against rivals who win business by overbilling. The committee's amendments narrowing the original "excessive profit" language reduced the risk of reaching lawful pricing.
